answer.decision: Adopt tail-aware sampling that retains all error traces and very slow requests, with a lower random sample of normal successful traffic.
answer.action: Deploy the validated tail sampler using rules that retain 100% of error and p99-latency traces and randomly sample normal traffic; monitor stored volume, cost reduction, rule accuracy, and per-service sample sufficiency for latency analysis.
reasons: The prototype reduced stored trace volume by 55%, exceeding the required 40% cost reduction target.
It retained all injected error and p99 test traces, directly satisfying the diagnostic-retention constraint.
Errors are only 0.7% of requests but provide 46% of traces used in incident reviews, so uniform or head-based sampling risks discarding disproportionately valuable evidence.
Normal successful traffic exceeds 98% of volume, making it the appropriate category for aggressive random sampling.
Independent, fully aggregated metrics preserve broad service-level latency analysis, while sampled normal traces provide request-level examples.
The backend supports retention decisions after spans are assembled, so tail-aware sampling is technically feasible.
assumptions: Stored trace-volume reduction translates approximately into telemetry cost reduction and remains at least 40% in production.
The p99 threshold is the intended definition of a very slow request.
The normal-traffic sampling rate will be configured high enough to produce representative per-service latency samples, especially for low-volume services.
Tail-sampler processing capacity and buffering are sufficient for peak production volume.
risks: Low-volume services may retain too few normal traces for statistically useful trace-level latency analysis unless minimum or adaptive sampling rates are used.
Tail-sampling buffers can add operational complexity, memory pressure, or trace loss during overload.
Production traffic distributions may differ from the prototype and reduce savings below the target.
Incorrect error or latency classification could discard valuable traces; configuration should be continuously validated.

citations.claim: The prototype reduced stored trace volume by 55% while retaining all injected error and p99 test traces.
Errors are 0.7% of requests but account for 46% of traces used during incident reviews.
Requests above the p99 latency threshold represent 1% of volume.
Normal successful traffic represents more than 98% of trace volume.
Metrics are independently collected at full aggregation and do not require retaining every trace.
The backend supports tail-based retention decisions after spans are assembled.
